Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA View image in fullscreen Aftermath of the Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: North Korean missiles hit Zaporizhzhia in deadly attack Zelenskyy warns Putin will use Russian election, in which opposition to the war is banned, as pretext for major call-up of troops. What we know on day 1,631 Warren Murray and agencies Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.22 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian forces used ballistic missiles supplied by North Korea , Ukraine’s president said, in an attack on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia where the Metinvest steel company said seven civilian workers at its plant were killed and 21 injured. Three more civilians, including a 15-year-old boy, were killed by Russian drones and artillery in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, authorities said. Russia used missiles, drones and glide bombs to attack Ukrainian cities on Tuesday, said Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the president. One strike hit the grounds of a children’s hospital, leaving two craters but not hurting anyone, the State Emergency Service said. Ukraine’s military general staff said its forces struck an oil refinery in the city of Orsk in Russia’s Orenburg region near the border with Kazakhstan, about 1,500km (930 miles) from Ukraine, causing a fire. The refinery can process about 44m barrels of crude oil a year to produce gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel and other products. The Russian online retailer Wildberries said its logistical facilities in the Voronezh region of Russia near the Ukrainian border came under attack and caught fire . Romania’s defence ministry said its navy destroyed two suspected Russian drones drifting in the Black Sea about 90 nautical miles (166km) from the port of Constanta. The Gerbera-type drones – a cut-price Russian version of the Shahed – were blown up by divers and some pieces were recovered, the ministry said, adding that Ukraine said the drones were not theirs. Russia is aiming to exploit Kyiv’s critical shortage of Patriot air defence interceptors that can stop ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, adding that Moscow is preparing to recruit more troops for a new push on the frontline. “Every step Russia takes – increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilisation – all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation,” Zelenskyy posted. He was warned in recent days that North Korea is preparing to send up to 50,000 more troops to Russia. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence suggested Russia would use its “pseudo-election” in September as a pretext to declare a new mobilisation . Mobilisation involves the use of reservists and conscripts, which in 2022 led to protests in Russia such as recruiting offices being set on fire. “They are preparing for mobilisation in the autumn, ​immediately after the imitation of parliamentary elections,” Zelenskyy said as part of a plan to “ create the appearance that Russians supposedly support the war ”. Russia’s supreme ​court on Monday barred the Yabloko party , the only officially registered party that opposes Moscow’s ​war in Ukraine, from competing ‌in the election. Zelenskyy continued: “Then, following the so-called election, he plans an additional rapid mobilisation of several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year, plus another similar number next year.” Zelenskyy said Ukraine had ⁠ handed proposals to US ⁠negotiators for a plan ​to end the war with Moscow. Zelenskyy offered no details on the proposals. US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were last in Moscow in January and have not yet visited Kyiv . The Institute for the Study of War, a US thinktank, has said in an analysis that the Kremlin will not seriously negotiate as long as Putin believes he might still reach his full objectives. “Ukraine’s Patriot shortages offer Russia an opportunity to cause very serious damage to Ukraine over the coming winter and will therefore contribute to delaying meaningful negotiations and protracting the war.” The UN estimates that more than 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during the war are still being “deprived of their liberty” , with many held incommunicado and on grounds that don’t comply with international law. “Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment” of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, including sexual violence, said Claudia Fuentes Julio, the UN assistant secretary general for human rights. https://www.dw.com/en/frankfurt-airport-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JQZU Anopheles mosquitoes are most active between dusk and dawn, which can make bites easy to miss Image: Roger Eritja/Visually/picture alliance Advertisement At least one Frankfurt Airport employee has died after contracting malaria in an outbreak believed to have been caused by an infected mosquito brought into Germany on an aircraft. Germany's DPA news agency reported that another airport employee had died of malaria in July, citing Frankfurt's health authorities. At the time, the cause of death was not immediately clear. The case is part of a rare outbreak of so-called airport malaria , with six employees infected despite not having traveled to a malaria-risk country. What we know about the Frankfurt Airport malaria death Frankfurt Airport operator Fraport confirmed the latest death on Wednesday. A spokesperson said the company had been informed by the responsible health authority and expressed "deepest sympathy" to the employee's relatives. In total, six airport employees are known to have contracted so-called airport malaria in connection with their work. The first four infections became known in mid-July. Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI) for public health said those affected fell ill between July 4 and 6 and that the infections were believed to have been transmitted by an infected Anopheles mosquito imported by aircraft. What is airport malaria? Malaria cases in Germany normally involve people who have contracted the disease while traveling abroad. Airport malaria, however, can occur when an infected mosquito is transported on an aircraft or in luggage and then infects someone on the plane, at the airport or in the immediate surrounding area. Malaria research in Germany targets parasite’s life cycle To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The RKI describes such cases as very rare. The last documented case at Frankfurt Airport was in 2023. Because patients may not have traveled to a malaria-risk area, the disease can also be diagnosed later than usual. The remaining infected employees are receiving medical treatment, while the local health authority continues to monitor the situation. Mosquito traps have been installed at the airport. Mosquitoes captured there are being genetically analyzed at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp to determine their species and origin. Fraport has also informed employees at the airport and advised them to seek medical attention if they develop symptoms. https://gisuser.com/2026/09/british-poli.text: You are here: Home / *BLOG / Around the Web / British-Polish HR-tech firm CrawlJobs signs technology investment deal with JOBS.PL The agreement will support the redevelopment of Poland’s oldest online recruitment service and marks the first step in CrawlJobs’ wider international strategy. British-Polish HR-tech firm CrawlJobs.com has signed a technology investment agreement with JOBS.PL, one of Central Europe’s longest-established online recruitment platforms. The partnership will combine JOBS.PL’s recognised national brand with CrawlJobs’ technology and international reach. A new version of JOBS.PL is already in testing and is scheduled to launch at the end of August 2026. The companies describe the agreement as the first stage of a longer-term relationship intended to prepare JOBS.PL for future integration into the international CrawlJobs Group. Modernising a recruitment pioneer JOBS.PL was launched in March 1998 as the first online recruitment service in Poland and Central Europe. Over the following decades, it became one of the country’s most recognisable employment brands, used by more than 19,000 employers throughout its history. The platform currently publishes close to 10,000 job advertisements each month. Its position in the Polish market gives CrawlJobs access to a well-established employer network, while JOBS.PL gains the product, software and automation capabilities needed to compete in a recruitment market that has changed dramatically since the platform first launched. The technology investment is focused on rebuilding and modernising the service rather than replacing the identity that made JOBS.PL valuable. The refreshed platform is expected to improve the experience for both employers and candidates while creating the technical foundation for closer cooperation between the two businesses. A return to JOBS.PL The agreement also marks a return to JOBS.PL for CrawlJobs founder Simon Bodych, a former employee of the platform. More than a decade ago, he helped triple the site’s traffic and increase its revenue fivefold. He now returns as CEO of CrawlJobs and a technology investor in JOBS.PL, with a plan to bring the platform into the CrawlJobs Group. Connecting local trust with global technology CrawlJobs uses an AI-supported crawler to collect and organise vacancies published on company websites. The platform operates internationally and makes job opportunities available in 20 language versions, helping candidates discover roles that may otherwise remain spread across thousands of separate employer career pages. In July 2026, CrawlJobs recorded close to 20,000 candidate registrations, according to the company. Its expansion strategy is based on combining this global infrastructure with established recruitment platforms that already possess strong recognition and employer relationships in their domestic markets. That approach reflects a wider challenge in online recruitment. Hiring is increasingly international, but job markets remain highly local. Candidates may be willing to work remotely or relocate, yet employers still depend on national platforms, local language support and brands that have earned trust over many years. CrawlJobs’ model is intended to connect those two realities rather than forcing every market into a single, uniform platform. The first step in a wider international strategy The JOBS.PL agreement is the first deal announced under CrawlJobs’ strategy of working with recognised recruitment services in different countries. For the British-Polish company, Poland offers a natural starting point: it combines a sizeable employment market with the opportunity to modernise one of the region’s original online recruitment brands. The immediate priority is the launch of the new JOBS.PL platform at the end of August. Further integration is expected to follow gradually, with the companies concentrating first on technology, product development and the experience offered to employers and jobseekers. For JOBS.PL, the partnership opens a new chapter almost three decades after its launch. For CrawlJobs, it represents the transition from building a global recruitment platform to developing a broader international group – beginning with the service where its founder’s own journey in the industry started.
